title: CAF for Aviation (CAP1850) Assessment
edition: adapted from NCSC core CAF v3.0 (CAP1850, 2020)
framing: The CAF for Aviation is the CAA's outcome-based assessment, used at Stage 4 of the CAP1753 oversight process for Tier 1 and Tier 2 aviation organisations. It is adapted from version 3.0 of the NCSC core CAF and has 39 contributing outcomes across 14 principles and 4 objectives. Each outcome is judged Achieved, Partially Achieved or Not Achieved, or marked Not relevant. The CAA issues each organisation an expected profile for its tier, and the assessment is the basis for an ASSURE Cyber Audit and Certificate of Compliance. The aviation framework is separate from NCSC CAF 4.0, which has 41 outcomes and different principle wording.
sourceNote: Objective / principle / outcome structure and aviation-specific principle descriptions extracted from CAP1850 (CAF for Aviation guidance) and NCSC core CAF v3.0. The per-outcome Indicators of Good Practice (IGPs) live in the CAF for Aviation workbook and are EMPTY slots here, to be populated from that official source. stateSummary and otLens are empty first-draft slots. Source: CAA CAP1850 (CAF for Aviation), Crown copyright; built on NCSC CAF v3.0.

objectives.name: Minimising the impact of cyber security incidents

principles.name: Governance
principles.description: The organisation has appropriate management policies and processes in place to govern its approach to the security of critical systems.

principles.name: Risk management
principles.description: The organisation takes appropriate steps to identify, assess and understand security risks to the critical systems supporting the operation of essential functions, including an overall organisational approach to risk management.

principles.name: Asset management
principles.description: Everything required to deliver, maintain or support critical systems is determined and understood, including data, people and systems, as well as supporting infrastructure such as power or cooling.

principles.name: Supply chain
principles.description: The organisation understands and manages security risks to critical systems that arise from dependencies on external suppliers, including ensuring appropriate measures where third-party services are used.

principles.name: Function protection policies and processes
principles.description: The organisation defines, implements, communicates and enforces appropriate policies and processes that direct its overall approach to securing critical systems and data that support operation of essential functions.

principles.name: Identity and access control
principles.description: The organisation understands, documents and manages access to critical systems. Users (or automated functions) that can access critical data or systems are appropriately verified, authenticated and authorised.

principles.name: Data security
principles.description: Data stored or transmitted electronically is protected from unauthorised access, modification or deletion that may cause an adverse impact on critical systems, including information that would assist an attacker such as design details of critical systems.

principles.name: System security
principles.description: Critical systems and technology critical for the operation of essential functions are protected from cyber attack, using robust and reliable protective security measures informed by an organisational understanding of risk.

principles.name: Resilient networks and systems
principles.description: The organisation builds resilience against cyber attack and system failure into the design, implementation, operation and management of critical systems.

principles.name: Staff awareness and training
principles.description: Staff have appropriate awareness, knowledge and skills to carry out their organisational roles effectively in relation to the security of critical systems supporting the operation of essential functions.

principles.name: Security monitoring
principles.description: The organisation monitors the security status of the networks and systems supporting the operation of critical systems in order to detect potential security problems and to track the ongoing effectiveness of protective security measures.

principles.name: Proactive security event discovery
principles.description: The organisation detects, within critical systems, malicious activity affecting or with the potential to affect the operation of essential functions, even when the activity evades standard signature-based solutions or when such solutions are not deployable.

principles.name: Response and recovery planning
principles.description: There are well-defined and tested incident management processes in place that aim to ensure continuity of essential functions in the event of system or service failure, with mitigation activities to contain or limit the impact of compromise.

principles.name: Lessons learned
principles.description: When an incident occurs, steps are taken to understand its root causes and to ensure appropriate remediating action is taken to protect against future incidents.

outcomes.title: Board direction
outcomes.stateSummary: The board sets and owns the direction for securing critical systems. Cyber risk is visible at board level and is treated as a matter for the whole organisation.
outcomes.rationale: Without board ownership, the security of critical systems competes with other priorities for attention and funding, and usually loses. In aviation, cyber risk can affect safety, so ownership needs to sit with the board. The CAA looks for evidence that the board governs cyber risk and keeps it under review after delegating the work.

outcomes.title: Roles and responsibilities
outcomes.stateSummary: Security roles and responsibilities for critical systems are clearly defined and assigned, including the Accountable Manager and Cyber Security Responsible Manager that CAP1753 requires.
outcomes.rationale: Security often falls into the gap between functions, and CAP1753 requires named accountable roles. With clear responsibilities, a named person owns the security of each critical system.

outcomes.title: Decision-making
outcomes.stateSummary: Decisions affecting the security of critical systems are made by people who understand both the cyber risk and the operational and safety consequences.
outcomes.rationale: Decisions about critical systems must weigh cyber risk and the operational and safety consequences together. When security and operational decisions are taken separately, controls end up unsuited to the operation, or risks are accepted without anyone accountable signing them off.

outcomes.title: Risk management process
outcomes.stateSummary: A defined, repeatable risk-management process identifies, assesses and treats risks to the critical systems supporting essential functions, with risk ownership and a maintained risk register.
outcomes.rationale: Critical systems cannot be defended against risks that have not been identified. Without a risk process, effort goes wherever the loudest voice points. A defined process keeps the protection of essential functions proportionate and justified.

outcomes.title: Assurance
outcomes.stateSummary: The organisation obtains independent assurance that its view of security risk is accurate and has been challenged.
outcomes.rationale: An organisation can believe its risk is well managed until an incident proves otherwise. Independent assurance finds the gaps between documented controls and day-to-day practice before an attacker does.

outcomes.title: Asset management
outcomes.stateSummary: Everything needed to deliver and support critical systems is identified, recorded and kept current. This includes data, people, systems and supporting infrastructure such as power and cooling.
outcomes.rationale: Critical systems cannot be protected, patched or monitored if no one knows they exist, and aviation environments build up legacy and supporting infrastructure over decades. Almost every other outcome depends on a complete and current asset record.

outcomes.title: Supply chain
outcomes.stateSummary: Security risks arising from external suppliers and third-party services to critical systems are understood and managed, with cyber requirements placed on critical suppliers.
outcomes.rationale: Suppliers and third-party services provide components for critical systems and often hold standing access to them, so a trusted relationship can become an attack path. Supplier risk management covers one of the most direct routes into essential functions.

outcomes.title: Policy and process development
outcomes.stateSummary: Policies and processes that direct how critical systems and their data are secured are developed and documented.
outcomes.rationale: Policy sets out in advance how the organisation will secure critical systems. Without it, protection depends on individual memory and varies by person and shift, and the organisation cannot demonstrate it to a regulator.

outcomes.title: Policy and process implementation
outcomes.stateSummary: Those policies and processes are implemented and followed in practice.
outcomes.rationale: A policy that is not followed protects nothing. The CAA audits what is done in practice, and exposure is usually found in the gap between written policy and practice.

outcomes.title: Identity verification, authentication and authorisation
outcomes.stateSummary: Users and automated functions accessing critical systems or data are verified, authenticated and authorised appropriately, including for physical, remote and privileged access.
outcomes.rationale: Access control starts with verifying who and what accesses critical systems. Shared or unauthenticated access is common in operational settings and weakens that control. The rest of the protection depends on sound authentication and authorisation.

outcomes.title: Device management
outcomes.stateSummary: Devices that connect to critical systems are known and managed, so unmanaged or transient equipment cannot introduce risk unnoticed.
outcomes.rationale: Threats often reach otherwise controlled critical systems through unmanaged and transient devices. Knowing and managing the devices that connect closes a frequent route in.

outcomes.title: Privileged user management
outcomes.stateSummary: Privileged access to critical systems is tightly controlled, granted only where needed and managed across its lifecycle.
outcomes.rationale: Privileged accounts can change critical systems directly, so their compromise is among the most serious outcomes. Tight control of elevated access limits what an external attacker can do and the damage from a single mistake.

outcomes.title: Identity and access management
outcomes.stateSummary: Identity and access are managed across the joiner, mover and leaver lifecycle, so access stays in line with who needs it.
outcomes.rationale: Access that is granted and never reviewed builds up into standing risk, with old accounts and excess rights left in place. Managing the full identity lifecycle keeps access in line with what each person needs.

outcomes.title: Understanding data
outcomes.stateSummary: The organisation understands what critical data it holds and transmits, including information that would assist an attacker, and protects it accordingly.
outcomes.rationale: Data can only be protected in proportion once the organisation knows what it holds and why it matters. That includes information that would help an attacker map critical systems.

outcomes.title: Data in transit
outcomes.stateSummary: Data in transit across networks supporting critical systems is protected against interception and alteration. For control traffic, protection against alteration matters most.
outcomes.rationale: Data crossing networks that support critical systems can be intercepted or altered. Altered data reaching an operational system has physical consequences, so protection in transit covers integrity as well as confidentiality.

outcomes.title: Stored data
outcomes.stateSummary: Stored critical data and the systems holding it are protected against unauthorised access, modification or deletion.
outcomes.rationale: Stored critical data is a target for theft, and for tampering that could hide or enable an attack. Protecting it at rest limits what an intruder gains from reaching a store and what they can change unnoticed.

outcomes.title: Mobile data
outcomes.stateSummary: Data on mobile and removable media is managed so it does not leak sensitive information or carry threats into critical systems.
outcomes.rationale: Data on mobile and removable media leaves the controlled environment, and such media are a known route for data loss and for malware. Managing them closes a gap that other protection leaves open.

outcomes.title: Media equipment sanitisation
outcomes.stateSummary: Media and equipment are sanitised before disposal or reuse, so retired kit does not hand over configuration, credentials or data.
outcomes.rationale: Equipment retired without sanitisation still holds configuration, credentials and network details that are useful to an attacker. Sanitising it stops decommissioned kit from giving away a map of critical systems.

outcomes.title: Secure by design
outcomes.stateSummary: Critical systems are designed with security built in from the start, including sound architecture and segregation.
outcomes.rationale: Security designed into critical systems from the start works far better than security added later, and aviation systems stay in service for a long time. Early choices about architecture and segregation shape resilience for years.

outcomes.title: Secure configuration
outcomes.stateSummary: Critical systems are securely configured and hardened, with unnecessary services and default settings removed.
outcomes.rationale: Default configurations favour ease of setup over security and leave unnecessary services exposed. Secure configuration reduces the attack surface of critical systems to what the operation needs.

outcomes.title: Secure management
outcomes.stateSummary: The management and administration of critical systems is secured, especially remote and privileged management access.
outcomes.rationale: Critical systems are configured and controlled through their management interfaces, so an attacker who compromises those interfaces gains control of the systems. Securing management access, especially remote access, protects the most powerful routes in.

outcomes.title: Vulnerability management
outcomes.stateSummary: Vulnerabilities in critical systems are found, assessed and addressed through a managed process, with patching and mitigation appropriate to an operational environment.
outcomes.rationale: Most breaches exploit known vulnerabilities that were never addressed. A managed process to find, assess and address them shortens the window attackers rely on. Where operational systems limit patching, the assessment and mitigation steps carry more weight.

outcomes.title: Resilience preparation
outcomes.stateSummary: The organisation has prepared for disruption to critical systems. It understands what essential functions need to keep running and what to do when they cannot.
outcomes.rationale: Resilience depends on preparing before a disruption happens. Knowing what essential functions need in order to keep running is often the difference between a contained event and a crisis.

outcomes.title: Design for resilience
outcomes.stateSummary: Critical systems are designed to stay resilient against cyber attack and failure, and to degrade in a safe and predictable way.
outcomes.rationale: A critical system designed to fail safe and degrade gracefully limits how far an attack or failure spreads. In aviation this bears directly on keeping operations safe while systems are degraded.

outcomes.title: Backups
outcomes.stateSummary: Critical systems, including their configuration and software, are backed up in a way that is protected, verified and demonstrably restorable.
outcomes.rationale: Backups are the last defence against destructive attacks, ransomware and serious error. For critical systems they must include configuration and software as well as data. Recovery can only be relied on when backups are verified and restorable.

outcomes.title: Cyber security culture
outcomes.stateSummary: The organisation has a positive security culture, and staff value and support the security of critical systems in their daily work.
outcomes.rationale: Culture decides what people do when no procedure quite fits. Staff who value the security of critical systems catch what controls miss. Staff who see it as someone else's problem weaken even good defences.

outcomes.title: Cyber security training
outcomes.stateSummary: Staff have the awareness, knowledge and skills their roles require in relation to the security of critical systems.
outcomes.rationale: People act securely when they know how, and roles that touch critical systems need relevant, current skills. Training helps staff take the right action in routine work and during an incident.

outcomes.title: Monitoring coverage
outcomes.stateSummary: Security monitoring covers the networks and systems supporting critical systems sufficiently to detect potential security problems.
outcomes.rationale: An attack cannot be detected where there is no monitoring, and gaps in coverage are blind spots an attacker can move through. Critical systems need adequate coverage before an attack can be noticed at all.

outcomes.title: Securing logs
outcomes.stateSummary: Logs are complete, trustworthy, correctly correlated and protected against alteration, with access attributable to unique users.
outcomes.rationale: Logs are only useful if they are complete and trustworthy, and attackers often alter them early on. Securing and correctly correlating logs preserves the evidence and keeps it reliable.

outcomes.title: Generating alerts
outcomes.stateSummary: Monitoring generates meaningful, timely alerts that prompt a person to act.
outcomes.rationale: Monitoring data is of no use if nothing prompts a person to look at it. Timely, meaningful alerts give the organisation a chance to respond before an intrusion becomes an incident.

outcomes.title: Identifying security incidents
outcomes.stateSummary: Real security incidents are reliably distinguished from background events so that the response can begin.
outcomes.rationale: Monitoring is only useful if real incidents can be told apart from the constant background of events. Without reliable identification, attacks are lost in the noise and the response never starts.

outcomes.title: Monitoring tools and skills
outcomes.stateSummary: The organisation has the monitoring tools, and skilled people who understand both security and operations, to make detection effective.
outcomes.rationale: Monitoring depends on the tools deployed and the people using them. In aviation those people must understand both security and the operational systems. Adequate tools and skilled analysts make detection work in practice.

outcomes.title: System abnormalities for attack detection
outcomes.stateSummary: The organisation can recognise abnormalities in critical systems that indicate attack, including activity that evades signature-based detection.
outcomes.rationale: Capable attackers deliberately evade signature-based detection, so they are found by recognising abnormal behaviour in critical systems. This is the last line of detection against the most serious threats.

outcomes.title: Proactive attack discovery
outcomes.stateSummary: The organisation actively searches critical systems for malicious activity and does not rely on automated detection alone.
outcomes.rationale: Proactive discovery assumes that prevention will sometimes fail and searches for an intruder who has got past automated defences. It is how an organisation finds a capable attacker who is trying to avoid triggering alerts.

outcomes.title: Response plan
outcomes.stateSummary: A well-defined incident response plan covers the lifecycle of an incident affecting critical systems, including roles, responsibilities and the operational decisions an aviation incident demands.
outcomes.rationale: A response plan prepared in advance allows fast, coordinated action under pressure. In aviation it must cover operational and safety decisions that a generic IT plan leaves out.

outcomes.title: Response and recovery capability
outcomes.stateSummary: The organisation can carry out response and recovery, with the people, tools and rehearsed procedures needed to restore essential functions.
outcomes.rationale: A plan helps only if the organisation can carry it out. People, tools and rehearsed procedures restore essential functions and limit how long they stay degraded.

outcomes.title: Testing and exercising
outcomes.stateSummary: Incident plans are tested and exercised under realistic conditions so that gaps are found before a live incident.
outcomes.rationale: A plan that has never been tested tends to fail on first use. Exercises under realistic conditions expose gaps and wrong assumptions while they are still cheap to fix.

outcomes.title: Incident root cause analysis
outcomes.stateSummary: After an incident, root causes are understood through routine analysis covering policy as well as technical issues.
outcomes.rationale: Understanding why an incident happened stops it recurring. Root cause analysis that covers policy as well as technical failure finds the underlying problem, so the fix lasts.

outcomes.title: Using incidents to drive improvements
outcomes.stateSummary: Lessons from incidents are fed back into controls and the response capability, driving continual improvement.
outcomes.rationale: An organisation that learns from incidents strengthens its defences, and one that does not repeats the same failures. Lessons fed back into controls and the response capability lead to lasting improvement.

_contentNote: 39 outcomes across 14 principles, 4 objectives, aviation-specific. stateSummary (what Achieved looks like) and rationale (why it matters) populated in house style. IGPs remain EMPTY pending the CAF for Aviation workbook - those are the authoritative assessment criteria and must come from that official source. otLens optional/empty.
_assessmentMechanics: Per CAP1850: Not Achieved if any one Not-Achieved IGP applies; Partially/Achieved only if all IGPs in that column apply and no Not-Achieved applies. Not relevant requires justification. Assessment is per critical system (the workbook provides up to 25 system tabs); organisational outcomes (e.g. A1) assessed once and referenced.
